Icelandic Logistics Companies Face Disruption Amid Ongoing Port Blockade

Reykjavik – Iceland’s transportation and logistics sector is grappling with widespread disruption this week following the sudden blockade of several key shipping ports in the southwest of the country, an escalation of a geopolitical dispute with a neighboring state. The blockade, enforced since Wednesday morning, has brought container and freight operations at Hafnarfjörður and Grundartangi to a near standstill, with local authorities warning of mounting delays and economic loss.

The measure, which includes the physical presence of vessels and port entry restrictions, has effectively halted the offloading and loading of cargo for multiple Icelandic logistics firms, including NorthSea Freight and FjordLink Logistics. According to the Icelandic Association of Transport Operators, more than 80 percent of scheduled shipments have been delayed or rerouted, with some perishable goods reportedly stranded at sea.

“We are doing everything in our power to mitigate the impact, but the situation is unprecedented,” said Guðmundur Stefánsson, spokesperson for NorthSea Freight. “Our customers are facing significant uncertainty, and our ability to honor delivery timelines is severely compromised.”

The blockade follows heightened diplomatic tensions over disputed fishing rights in the North Atlantic, though officials declined to comment on specifics. The Foreign Ministry has called for immediate negotiations, but as of this afternoon, no breakthrough had been reported.

Transport workers at the affected ports have expressed concern for their livelihoods as operations remain suspended. “We’re worried about our jobs and the knock-on effects if this goes on much longer,” said Elísabet Jónsdóttir, a warehouse supervisor at the Hafnarfjörður terminal. “This is the busiest time of year for us.”

Icelandic logistics analysts estimate that the sector is losing approximately ISK 250 million per day as shipments are delayed or redirected to less efficient ports in Akureyri and Seyðisfjörður. Many trucks and cargo vessels have been forced to idle, incurring additional storage costs and risking spoilage of time-sensitive goods.

The Icelandic Federation of Logistics Companies released a statement urging swift diplomatic resolution and warning that prolonged disruption could have “far-reaching consequences for the nation’s supply chain.” Meanwhile, contingency plans are being developed to shift some freight to air transport, though capacity constraints remain a challenge.

As the blockade enters its third day, industry leaders and government officials are monitoring the situation closely, with hopes for a diplomatic solution to restore critical transport and logistics services.
